cues.text: A Constitution Turned Against the Church
Mexico's 1917 Constitution, drafted after a decade of revolutionary upheaval, contained sweeping anticlerical provisions restricting the Church's property ownership and role in education.

It also limited the number of priests permitted to minister within the country, with these articles largely unenforced until President Plutarco Elías Calles moved in 1926 to apply them with full and deliberate severity.

Calles himself declared that as long as he remained president, the Constitution of 1917 would be enforced in full, regardless of what he dismissed as the complaints of sacristans and the overly pious.
Churches Closed Nationwide
On August 1, 1926, the so-called Calles Law took effect, closing every Catholic church in Mexico.
This effectively ended public worship across the entire country.

In response, the Mexican bishops, with Vatican approval, suspended all public religious services rather than accept government registration requirements they judged an unacceptable intrusion on the Church's own authority.
An Underground Priest, Photographed in Death
Among the priests who continued ministering in secret was Miguel Pro , a Jesuit ordained abroad who returned to Mexico City in disguise.

He celebrated Mass and administered the sacraments underground; falsely implicated in an assassination attempt against Calles's successor, Pro was executed by firing squad in November 1927 without trial.
His arms were deliberately stretched wide in the form of a cross as he faced his executioners, crying Viva Cristo Rey — "Long live Christ the King" — moments before he died.

Calles ordered the execution photographed, hoping the images would frighten Catholics into submission; instead, the photographs, published on the front pages of the nation's newspapers, had precisely the opposite effect.
Denied a Catholic funeral by government order, Pro's father instead recited the prayers over his son's body himself, as a crowd of some twenty thousand mourners gathered in defiant tribute.
A Fourteen-Year-Old's Martyrdom
Among the youngest victims of the persecution was José Sánchez del Río , a fourteen-year-old boy who had joined the Cristero forces as a flag-bearer.
He was captured, tortured — the soles of his feet cut and forced to walk on salt — and repeatedly pressured to renounce his faith or betray his fellow fighters.
He refused every demand, reportedly asking that his parents be told simply that he would see them again in heaven before he was killed.
An Armed Rebellion, and an Uneasy Peace
Frustrated by the government's refusal to relent, tens of thousands of ordinary Catholics across rural Mexico took up arms as Cristeros — "warriors for Christ."
They fought a bitter three-year civil conflict against government forces.
A negotiated truce brought the open fighting to a close in 1929.
Brokered with Vatican involvement, the truce did not include any actual repeal of the underlying anticlerical laws.
The government's own hoped-for victory in the propaganda war backfired so completely that Calles was eventually forced to ban Mexican newspapers.
The ban prevented them from printing further images of the executed priest, but could not undo the effect his own order had already set in motion.
Legacy
The Cristero War claimed an estimated ninety thousand lives, combatant and civilian alike.
The deeper persecution of the Mexican Church, though reduced in its most violent forms after 1929, would continue in various legal and administrative guises for decades afterward.
Pope John Paul II canonized twenty-five Mexican martyrs of this period in 2000, including José Sánchez del Río, and beatified Miguel Pro in 1988.
He honored a generation of Mexican Catholics — clergy and laity, adults and children alike — who chose fidelity to their faith over submission to a state determined to erase it from public life.
